mcqs.question: Why can a fixed-window rate limiter let roughly 2x its configured limit through in a short span, even though each individual window reports staying under the limit?
options: The counter overflows silently once it exceeds the limit value
Fixed window doesn't support per-user limits, only global ones
Token refill happens faster than the counter can reset

A client can send the full quota at the very end of one window and the full quota again right at the start of the next, and both windows individually look compliant even though the combined burst straddling the boundary is double the intended rate
mcqs.explanation: The reset-to-zero at each boundary is the root cause: it creates a moment where two full quotas can land within one real second, split across the reset. There's no overflow bug involved, fixed window works fine per-user, and the effect is unrelated to token refill, which is a token-bucket concept.

mcqs.question: Two threads both read a token count of 1, and both then decrement it, letting two requests through on a single remaining token. What class of bug is this?
options: A check-then-act race — the check (is a token available) and the act (decrement it) aren't performed as one atomic unit, so the world can change between them
An off-by-one error in the token bucket's capacity calculation
A memory leak from not releasing tokens after use
A clock-skew bug from unsynchronized server clocks
mcqs.explanation: This is the textbook check-then-act race: correctness at each individual step doesn't guarantee correctness when steps interleave across threads. It isn't an off-by-one in the capacity math, it has nothing to do with releasing memory, and clock skew is a distinct, network-level problem covered separately.

mcqs.question: Why wouldn't you default to a sliding log (storing every request timestamp per key) even though it gives the most precise rate-limiting decision?
options: Sliding log is less accurate at the window boundary than fixed window
Sliding log cannot support per-user or per-key limits
Its memory cost is O(n) per key — every request timestamp is retained — versus O(1) for token bucket or sliding-window-counter, which makes it expensive at scale despite being exact
Sliding log requires a distributed store and cannot run in a single process
mcqs.explanation: Sliding log is the most accurate of the four, not the least — its drawback is purely memory: every timestamp per key, which grows with request volume rather than staying constant. It works fine per-key and in a single process; the trade-off is memory cost against the O(1) approximations, not correctness or deployment topology.

mcqs.question: In a multi-instance deployment, why is resetting a fixed-window counter based on each server's own local clock risky?
options: Local clocks are always slower than a shared store's clock
It's actually safe as long as each server is internally consistent with itself
Fixed windows can only be implemented using a shared clock, never a local one

Even small clock skew between servers means they don't reset at the same real moment, producing an inconsistent effective window across the deployment and risking double-counts or dropped windows if the design later centralizes
mcqs.explanation: Internal consistency on one server doesn't help once clients are routed across servers with skewed clocks — the effective window becomes inconsistent between instances. Skew direction isn't reliably 'always slower,' and fixed windows can be implemented with either a local or shared clock; the risk specifically comes from relying on unsynchronized local time across multiple servers.

mcqs.question: When moving a rate limiter's counter into Redis for a multi-server deployment, why is a Lua script or `INCR`+`EXPIRE` preferred over the app reading the count, deciding, then writing it back?
options: Lua scripts and INCR run faster on the network than a simple GET

Read-modify-write from the app reintroduces the exact check-then-act race from the single-process case, now across the network instead of across threads — the increment-and-check must be atomic inside the store itself
Redis doesn't support plain GET and SET commands
INCR and EXPIRE eliminate the need for a shared store entirely
mcqs.explanation: The failure mode is identical to the single-process race, just relocated: two app instances can both read the same count before either writes back, letting both proceed. Doing the increment (and expiry) atomically inside Redis closes that gap. Redis fully supports GET/SET; the issue is architectural, not about raw network speed, and a shared store is still required either way.
